Pommels
PUM-elz
noun
From Old French pomel, a little apple or rounded knob (Latin pomum, an apple), rendering the Hebrew gullah, a bowl or rounded basin. It names the swelling globe-like tops set upon the two brazen pillars of Solomon’s temple.

Biblical Definition

The pommels were the rounded, bowl-like crowns wrought atop the two great pillars, Jachin and Boaz, that stood before Solomon’s temple. In the temple record they are named among Huram’s brass work: “the two pillars, and the pommels, and the chapiters which were on the top of the two pillars, and the two wreaths to cover the two pommels of the chapiters” (2Ch 4:12). Four hundred pomegranates were set on the wreaths that covered them (2Ch 4:13), and the same objects are called “the two bowls of the chapiters” in the parallel account (1Ki 7:41-42). A pommel was thus the swelling globe upon the pillar-head, a rounded ornament of cast brass, crowned and netted and hung with pomegranates. Small as the word is, it belongs to the careful record of a house built wholly by pattern, where nothing was left to the workman’s fancy but all was made as the LORD had shown. The two pillars stood as pledges of establishment — Jachin, “He shall establish,” and Boaz, “In it is strength” — and their crowning pommels were the finished ornament of that stability. So the Scripture stoops to name the very knops and bowls of God’s house, that we might learn how exact and how beautiful is the order of the temple He builds, and how He crowns His pillars with comeliness as well as strength.

Webster 1828 Definition

The rounded, bowl-shaped ornaments crowning the tops of the two brazen pillars of Solomon’s temple.

expand to see more

POMMELS, the rounded knobs or globes set upon the chapiters of the two pillars before Solomon’s temple.

They are also called the bowls of the chapiters in the parallel record of the Kings.

They were of cast brass, covered with wreaths or networks and hung with pomegranates.

The word comes from the Old French for a little apple, a swelling rounded top.

They belonged to the ornamental crowning of the pillars Jachin and Boaz.

Key Scripture

2Ch 4:12 — "To wit, the two pillars, and the pommels, and the chapiters which were on the top of the two pillars, and the two wreaths to cover the two pommels of the chapiters which were on the top of the pillars;"

2Ch 4:13 — "And four hundred pomegranates on the two wreaths; two rows of pomegranates on each wreath, to cover the two pommels of the chapiters which were upon the pillars."

1Ki 7:41 — "The two pillars, and the two bowls of the chapiters that were on the top of the two pillars; and the two networks, to cover the two bowls of the chapiters which were upon the top of the pillars;"

1Ki 7:42 — "And four hundred pomegranates for the two networks, even two rows of pomegranates for one network, to cover the two bowls of the chapiters that were upon the pillars;"

Modern Corruption

An ornament of the temple, not a contested doctrine; it recovers the exactness and comeliness of the house God builds by pattern.

expand to see more

The pommels rebuke the careless spirit that despises detail in the worship and house of God. The age counts such things trifling — a knob upon a pillar, a bowl of brass — and would build the church by its own convenience rather than by the given pattern. But the Scripture that names the pommels teaches that God is not indifferent to the fashion of His house, and that beauty and order there are matters of His own command.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God builds by exact pattern and crowns His pillars with comeliness. The two pillars pledged establishment and strength; their rounded pommels were the finished ornament of that stability. So in the true temple, Christ’s church, He joins strength to beauty and leaves nothing to the fancy of men.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The rounded bowl-like crowns of the temple pillars, ornament of a house built wholly by God’s pattern.

expand to see more

Pommels — the rounded globe-like tops of the two brazen pillars of the temple (2Ch 4:12).

They are called the bowls of the chapiters in the parallel account (1Ki 7:41).

The word is from Old French pomel, a little apple or rounded knob.

They were covered with wreaths and hung with four hundred pomegranates (2Ch 4:13).

They crowned the pillars Jachin and Boaz, pledges of establishment and strength.

Usage

"Even the pommels of the pillars were made by the pattern God showed, not the workman’s fancy."

"God crowned His pillars with comeliness as well as strength."

"Scripture stoops to name the knops and bowls of His house, that we learn its exact order."
